definition: Software that runs as part of a device’s particular function. It may run directly with hardware support or under an operating system.
The program and associated data stored for a device to execute. Many devices provide a supported way to replace firmware; the name does not mean that updates are impossible.
A chip combining one or more processor cores, memory and hardware interfaces for controlling a device. A board using it may add external memory and other components.
A processor’s instruction-execution engine. A microcontroller may contain more than one core, so one foreground loop does not imply that nothing else can execute.
Working memory whose contents are not retained when its power is removed. Ordinary SRAM is an example; its contents are not a persistent record of application data.
Memory that can retain stored contents without continuous power. Flash and manufacturer boot ROM serve different roles even though both can retain data.
Non-volatile memory that supports programming and erasure through its specified interface. A microcontroller may have internal flash or access a separate flash chip.
Static random-access memory: the type of working RAM provided by many microcontrollers. Its stored data is volatile, so retaining data through power loss requires a different supported mechanism.
A dedicated hardware block, such as a timer or serial controller, that software configures and uses to exchange signals or perform a hardware function.
A description of what each address range represents, such as RAM, program storage or peripheral registers. Different ranges can have different access behaviour.
A hardware interface location used to control or observe a device function. Reads and writes can have documented side effects, so it is not automatically interchangeable with ordinary RAM.

An application arrangement without an operating system managing application execution; a real-time operating system also counts as an operating system. Startup code, libraries, interrupts and other hardware support may still execute.
A requirement that a result or response occur within a specified timing constraint. Producing the correct value after that constraint can still be a failure.
The manufacturer’s technical description of a component’s functions, operating conditions and limits. It describes the component, not every board built around it.
A circuit drawing showing components and their electrical connections. It helps establish how a particular board uses a chip’s pins and interfaces.
A circuit board designed to make a processor or microcontroller easier to power, program and connect during development. Its components and wiring depend on the exact model.
Software development kit: libraries, headers, examples and build support for developing software for a supported target. Its board configuration must match the intended hardware.
Build settings describing the supported board target and its hardware choices. Selecting the wrong board can choose an unsuitable pin or peripheral implementation.
A particular hardware version of a circuit board. Check its own documentation because components or connections can change between revisions.
An electrical connection on a component. Its supported functions and electrical limits come from the device documentation, while the board determines what is connected to it.
Application programming interface: the supported functions and conventions through which code uses a library or component. An API’s existence does not override hardware operating limits.
Light-emitting diode: a component that emits light when driven appropriately. An onboard LED can be a documented firmware observation point; its controlling connection varies by board.
The name used for the boot-selection control in the documented Pico programming workflow. Holding it during the specified startup procedure enters a supported programming interface.
Universal Serial Bus: a standard interface used by many computers and devices. A target’s USB programming support depends on its actual hardware and boot software.
A firmware file format accepted by certain supported bootloaders, including the documented Pico USB programming route. It is not a universal format accepted by every microcontroller.
The collection of tools used to translate, combine and inspect a program for a target. A firmware project commonly uses a compiler, linker and additional programming or debugging tools.
A compiler that runs on one system while producing code for another target. The compiler’s target must match the intended processor and software environment.
The human-readable program given to development tools. Saving source changes the file on the development computer; it does not itself program a device.
An intermediate file produced by translation, usually containing machine code, data and information the linker needs to combine program parts. It is not necessarily a complete firmware image.
A tool that combines translated program parts and libraries, resolves references between them and lays out the resulting program according to the build configuration.
A source file commonly included to share declarations and other definitions with C source files. Including a declaration does not by itself supply every required function implementation.
The C toolchain stage that handles preprocessing directives such as header inclusion before compilation proper. It is separate from linking translated object files.
A built representation of the program prepared for the target and a supported transfer method. Its processor target, memory layout and required file format must match the device workflow.
The processor and software environment for which the toolchain produces a program. A successful build for one target does not establish that another can execute it.
An event that restarts execution through the device’s documented reset path. Reset does not inherently replace stored firmware or promise that every memory region is erased.
Startup code entered through the processor’s reset path. In the described CMSIS Cortex-M template it normally calls system initialisation before transferring control to the C runtime.
A processor value identifying the current stack location used by the execution environment. Cortex-M startup includes an initial stack-pointer value.
A table identifying the handlers for processor exceptions and device interrupts in the described Cortex-M model. Its actual entries and placement follow the target’s rules.

Supporting code that establishes the C execution environment and supplies language-library support. The described CMSIS startup path transfers to runtime initialisation before calling the application main function.
Code that loads or starts another program and may provide a programming or recovery interface. Its capabilities and entry method are specific to the device.
Read-only memory. In the RP2040 example, manufacturer boot code resides in ROM rather than in the updateable application image.
The repeated foreground sequence that services an application’s jobs. In a cooperative arrangement, each job must return control for later foreground jobs to run.
An arrangement where foreground jobs allow other foreground work to proceed by returning control. It does not prevent interrupts or prove a timing bound.
A model that records a current state and defines how inputs cause transitions to another state. An explicit transition rule can be traced and tested independently of hardware.

An event- or condition-driven step defined by a state machine, which can change its current state. A self-transition returns to the same state. Testing these steps checks the model's behaviour, not the physical hardware.

A hardware action caused by reading or writing a peripheral register, beyond storing or retrieving an ordinary RAM value. For example, a documented read may remove an item from a hardware data queue; access must follow the device manual.
A discrete accepted occurrence of a button press. It differs from repeatedly observing that a button is still held down.
A tool used to observe and control program execution, such as stopping at a chosen instruction or inspecting state through a supported debug connection.
A hardware-supported connection used by development tools to inspect, control or program a target. Available interfaces and their electrical requirements vary by device and board.
A region of working memory used to hold data while it is produced, consumed or transferred. A buffer’s existence does not imply persistent storage.
A hardware-supported request that can transfer processor execution to a handler when the processor’s rules and configuration permit. It can occur between foreground instructions.

Common Microcontroller Software Interface Standard: Arm’s collection of interfaces, software components and tools for supported processors. Its Cortex-M startup template is one documented startup model, not a rule for every MCU.
An Arm processor-core family intended for microcontroller systems. A chip using one of these cores also has vendor-specific memory and peripheral details.
A Raspberry Pi microcontroller used as a concrete illustration in this course. Its on-chip SRAM, external flash interface and boot ROM are device-specific features.
A device or part of a device whose computing hardware and software perform a particular function. Its software may run with or without an operating system.
